Attorney Ben Crump on legal questions surrounding fatal Six Flags roller coaster incident – WABE
Attorney Ben Crump on legal questions surrounding fatal Six Flags roller coaster incident
Cobb County
Law
Law Enforcement
News
Attorney Ben Crump on legal questions surrounding fatal Six Flags roller coaster incident
Cobb County
Jim Burress
| WABE
October 16th, 2026
Attractions are seen at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles (24 kilometers) northwest of Atlanta, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (AP Photo/Mike Stewart)
Many questions remain unanswered after 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died after being ejected from the Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Oct. 12. State officials are investigating the incident, including how the ride operated and whether it followed safety requirements.
Civil rights attorney Ben Crump says some of the answers families seek after amusement park deaths may emerge through litigation. While Crump is best known for representing families in high-profile civil rights cases, his firm has also represented families in lawsuits involving fatal amusement park rides.
That includes the family of 14-year-old Tyre Sampson, who died after falling from the FreeFall drop tower at Orlando’s ICON Park in 2022. In 2024, a jury awarded Sampson’s family $310 million in a lawsuit against the ride’s manufacturer.
When WABE’s “All Things Considered” spoke with Crump, he said he had not been hired to represent Kariem’s family, but he discussed the questions he looks for in amusement park death cases, including whether safety procedures were followed, what the evidence can reveal about how an incident occurred, and how families can pursue accountability.
Christopher Alston contributed to this report.

Federal judge questions harm in relocating detainees to South Georgia – WABE
Federal judge questions harm in relocating detainees to South Georgia
Crime
Criminal Justice
Justice System
Local
Federal judge questions harm in relocating detainees to South Georgia
Criminal Justice
Chamian Cruz
| WABE
October 16th, 2026
Natasha Perdew Silas, executive director of the Northern District of Georgia's Federal Defender Program, speaks at a news conference outside the Richard B. Russel Federal Building on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (Chamian Cruz/WABE)
A federal judge in Atlanta appeared skeptical on Friday of arguments that U.S. Marshals are relocating pretrial detainees at a distance that violates their constitutional rights.
The court hearing also revealed that nearly all 400 of those individuals are already at the Irwin County Detention Center in South Georgia.
Last week, the Northern District of Georgia’s Federal Defender Program filed a lawsuit against the U.S. Marshals Service to prevent just that from happening.
Attorneys for the defender program told U.S. District Judge Mark Cohen they can’t properly prepare for hearings when their clients are roughly 200 miles from Atlanta’s federal courthouse.
But Cohen repeatedly questioned whether he had the authority to tell the Marshals Service not to cancel its contract with the Robert A. Deyton Detention Facility (RADD) in Clayton County, which he also called not exactly “the Taj Mahal.”
Also, because the defender program so far has only one detainee alleging he isn’t getting his mail following the move, Cohen said it’d be a “hard row to hoe” to get him to issue a temporary restraining order, adding that the lawsuit has only made it harder to communicate with Marshals and resolve issues.
“None of us wanted what happened with RADD to happen, but it happened, and we’re all trying to deal with it,” Cohen said.
The Marshals Service hasn’t explained its decision, especially since the Irwin County facility has faced allegations of medical abuse, but pointed to its ability to provide private telephone and videoconference rooms to facilitate confidential attorney-client communications,” according to court filings.
Nathan Kitchens, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Georgia, told WABE last week that they’re monitoring conditions at the Irwin County facility.
“We are in fact going to be touring the facility… with defense counsel to ensure that the U.S. Marshals Service is meeting those commitments that they’ve made,” Kitchens said.

articles.title: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving the job after a rocky start
articles.text:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving the job after a rocky start – WABE
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving the job after a rocky start
Donald Trump
National News
Politics
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving the job after a rocky start
National News
Associated Press
AP
October 16th, 2026
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia walks out to speak with reporters in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Washington.
Julia Demaree Nikhinson / AP
Katie Zacharia is departing as White House press secretary, a person familiar with the matter said Friday, after a short and rocky tenure that was defined by questions about her professional background and lack of polish in fielding questions from journalists.
The person, granted anonymity to discuss a personnel decision not yet made public, said Zacharia would be transitioning out of the role. The shift comes after President Donald Trump cast significant doubt on her future earlier Friday, telling reporters that he would have a discussion with her following his weekend travel — and that if he were her, he would reconsider the job.
Zacharia had come under immediate scrutiny when she appeared uncomfortable during her inaugural briefing on Tuesday, delivering halting remarks touting the president and his accomplishments. Her 14-minute briefing was followed by criticism that the conservative commentator had long called herself a lawyer when she had not passed a bar exam nor was otherwise credentialed to practice.
Zacharia was a surprise choice when Trump announced her appointment on Oct. 9, as the successor to Karoline Leavitt, the youngest-ever White House press secretary who had been part of Trump’s inner circle for years. The chaos surrounding her appointment was reminiscent of some of Trump’s short-lived staff picks from his first term.
Trump said he told Zacharia that she might want to change her mind about the job, and said he thought she had been treated unfairly by the press.
“I told her, ‘I think you’re better off being happy,’” Trump told reporters on the White House lawn as he left for a rally in Georgia. “I said, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider.’ I said, ‘You think about it, but I would reconsider.’”
Messages to Zacharia seeking comment were not returned on Friday, and the White House offered no immediate comment.
In his own comments, Trump said he told his press secretary, “‘Katie, do you need this? I don’t think you need this,’” and that he wanted “her to have a good life” and not be subjected to criticism, which he likened to being “brutalized by the media.”
The president said he’d make a final determination later, perhaps after his campaign travel on Friday and this weekend, adding, “When I get back, we’re gonna talk.” He was asked who might replace Zacharia, and said that there were a lot of people who wanted the job.
Zacharia’s first official day on the job was Monday
In Zacharia’s first and only briefing on Tuesday, she took questions from just three reporters, all from conservative-leaning or Trump-friendly outlets, and left after only about 14 minutes.
Zacharia has said she wanted to keep her briefing short to ensure Trump had enough time later that morning for his own question-and-answer session with reporters, and that she had not been fully briefed by White House staff beforehand.
She later traveled with Trump when he held rallies on Wednesday and Thursday in Alaska, Arizona and Montana — but did not hold more press briefings.
In an appearance on Fox News Channel earlier Friday, Zacharia was asked if she had the president’s confidence and responded: “I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me.” But she also wouldn’t say when her next press briefing might be.
Questions about why Zacharia called herself a lawyer
Zacharia, a Pepperdine University law graduate, also faced criticism for describing herself as a lawyer when appearing as a commentator on conservative television outlets. Zacharia said the term was a proper one to use when she was offering legal analysis, and said she had worked as a lawyer in China.
Zacharia said Friday on Fox News that she wasn’t asked about passing the bar before becoming press secretary, and Trump noted in his subsequent comments that she was hired as a spokesperson for the White House, not as an attorney.
Before joining the White House, Zacharia had been working in communications for Trump Media, the company that oversees the president’s social media site, Truth Social. She also briefly worked at the Department of Homeland Security during the second Trump administration.

articles.title: Court lifts block on GA law restricting children’s social media access
articles.text:
Court lifts block on GA law restricting children’s social media access
Court lifts block on Georgia law that restricts children’s access to social media
Kids
Law
Court lifts block on Georgia law that restricts children’s access to social media
Law
Ty Tagami
Capitol Beat
October 16th, 2026
The Fulton County Superior Courthouse is seen, Thursday, March 14, 2024, in Atlanta. (AP Photo/Mike Stewart)
Georgia can enforce a 2024 state law that seeks to limit social media companies’ access to children under a new ruling by the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.
The Protecting Georgia’s Children on Social Media Act passed the General Assembly with broad bipartisan support, but an organization representing online platforms sued and secured a preliminary injunction last year.
On Thursday, a three-judge appellate panel voided the injunction after determining that NetChoice had failed to demonstrate that it was likely to succeed on its claims.
Georgia Attorney General Chris Carr, who defended the state, called the decision a major win for families.
“This is about keeping our children safe from online predators and mental health harms,” Carr said in a statement.
A brief filed by Carr’s office blamed social media for a litany of harms to minors, including rising rates of anxiety, body-image problems, depression, self-harm and suicide.
The dangers go beyond mental illness, Carr’s brief added.
“Bullying, intimidation, harassment, and sexual predation thrive on social media platforms,” it said.
The law at issue requires covered social media companies to make “commercially reasonable efforts” to verify users’ ages and mandates parental consent for those under 16 to open accounts. It also bans advertising to children when the ads are based on personal information other than age and location.
Senate Bill 351 passed the General Assembly in 2024. Gov. Brian Kemp signed it,  despite a request by NetChoice that he veto it.
NetChoice sued in May 2025, two months before the law was supposed to take effect.
The trade association represents companies and platforms, including Meta, YouTube, Reddit, X and Pinterest.
A federal judge in Atlanta issued a preliminary injunction against enforcement.
The June 2025  ruling by Judge Amy Totenberg of the Northern District of Georgia determined the industry group was likely to prevail on claims that the law violated the First Amendment’s free speech protections.
The appellate court opinion, written by Judge Kevin C. Newsom, said NetChoice had standing to sue. But it vacated the preliminary injunction and sent the case back to district court for further proceedings.
The  opinion found several flaws in NetChoice’s arguments, including that the organization had failed to account for the differing constitutional protections for the full range of speech and platforms the law regulates.
Newsom wrote that “it’s not necessarily true that social-media websites engage exclusively in ‘fully protected’ speech. The state contends (and no one seems to dispute) that some platforms, like X and Reddit, do host at least some pornography — which is protected for adults but, importantly, not for minors.”
The opinion referred to those companies’ products as “hybrid” platforms distinct from “conventional” platforms that host fully protected speech and from “rogue” platforms with “exclusively unprotected” speech.
NetChoice said it was evaluating its legal options and remained committed to fighting for free speech online in Georgia.
“While we are disappointed in the Eleventh Circuit’s ruling, the court notably did not hold that SB 351 is constitutional,” Paul Taske, Director of the NetChoice Litigation Center, said in a statement.
The decision comes amid a public criticism and civil lawsuits alleging that Meta’s platforms addict children and cause mental health harms.
In August, Georgia joined other states and jurisdictions in proposing a  multistate settlement of a lawsuit against the company, which operates Facebook and Instagram.
Carr participated in the suit with 46 other states, the District of Columbia and several U.S. territories.
The settlement would require up to $17.1 billion in payments by Meta, with up to $135 million going to Georgia. In addition, the settlement terms would require that Meta impose new limits on teen accounts while giving parents the option for more control.
This story was provided by WABE media partner Capitol Beat.

articles.title: Trump wants midterms all about him, Democrats happy to oblige
articles.text:
Trump wants midterms all about him, Democrats happy to oblige
Trump wants the midterms to be all about himself. Judging by the ads, Democrats are happy to oblige
Donald Trump
Election
Kids
Law
Trump wants the midterms to be all about himself. Judging by the ads, Democrats are happy to oblige
Donald Trump
Associated Press
AP
October 16th, 2026
President Trump speaks at Peterbilt Motors, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, in Denton, Texas. (Tony Gutierrez/AP)
Tony Gutierrez/AP
President Donald Trump says he wants voters to pretend that he’s on the ballot in this year’s midterm elections.
His rivals are doing their best to help his case.
Democratic candidates and their allies have spent more than $163 million since Sept. 1 on television advertising that mentions the Republican president, according to an Associated Press analysis of data from AdImpact, which charts media spending.
That includes airing ads that reference Trump on broadcast, cable and streaming nearly 180,000 times, the data shows. Republicans, meanwhile, have run ads that talk about the president just 16,000 times, at an estimated cost of $11 million, over the same period.
It’s a noticeable silence about the party’s dominant yet unpopular leader.
Many of the Democrats’ ads accuse Republican opponents of siding with the president over voters, particularly on issues like tariffs and the Iran war, which they blame for jacking up costs.
The ads include one from the campaign of Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who is running for reelection and has spent nearly $3 million on a Trump-focused ad attacking his rival, Rep. Mike Collins, for his close relationship with the president.
“Mike Collins voted for Trump’s war in Iran, sending gas prices through the roof. He voted for Trump’s tariffs, sending grocery prices soaring. And Mike Collins voted with Trump to double health insurance premiums for more than a million Georgians,” it says. “Mike Collins sides with Donald Trump and makes you pay more.”
Republican National Committee spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre said Democratic messaging reflected the party’s hollowness instead of its strength.
“Democrats are lighting money on fire talking about President Trump because they have no agenda other than investigation, obstruction and impeachment,” she said. “Trump Derangement Syndrome isn’t a policy platform, it’s a $160 million way of saying you have nothing to offer to the American people.”
Democrats link Trump and his allies to economic woes
Another ad from the House Majority PAC, a super PAC dedicated to electing Democrats to the House, opens with a middle-aged woman standing over her kitchen stove and talking about how her family is “barely getting by” before she expresses her disappointment in Pennsylvania Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, who is one of Republicans’ vulnerable incumbents.
“He used to be independent. But now it seems like he’s in lockstep with Donald Trump. It really bothers me,” she says, adding, “Congressman Fitzpatrick is not for us anymore.”
Indeed, all the Democratic ads that have aired in Pennsylvania’s tightly contested 1st Congressional District since Sept. 1 have mentioned Trump, even though Fitzpatrick voted against Trump’s tariffs and his power to wage war against Iran without congressional approval.
All four of the ads talking about Trump have aired a combined 2,000 times in that period, the AdImpact data shows. Fitzpatrick is being challenged by Democrat Bob Harvie, a county commissioner who is a former social studies teacher.
Democratic strategists say the messaging reflects the sentiment of voters.
“Every single poll and every single focus group shows affordability to be voters’ number one issue, and they specifically point to corrupt politicians as being responsible for driving up prices,” said House Majority PAC spokesperson Katarina Flicker.
Republican ads back away from the president
Out of dozens of issue categories tracked by AdImpact, the analysis found that Trump was the fourth most common issue mentioned by Democrats in House and Senate races’ final stretch. It was topped only by healthcare, taxes and accusations about opponents being beholden to special interests.
For Republicans in the same races, Trump-themed ads clocked in at number 33, by comparison. The top issues in their ads were taxes and crime.
Idaho Republican Senator Jim Risch tells viewers he “fought alongside President Trump to pass the biggest tax cuts for working families in American history.”
Overall in the race’s final stretch since Sept. 1, Democrats have spent or plan to spend $1.8 billion in ads across all federal, state and local elections. Republicans have spent or reserved $2.2 billion nationwide.
Republican strategist Alex Conant said Democrats are banking on Trump motivating their base to vote, an approach they’ve routinely used over the last decade.
“Democrats want this election to be a referendum on Trump. They want to equate a vote for a Republican candidate to a vote for Trump,” he said.
For Conant’s party, it’s a different calculus.
“We have a ton of money and we’re throwing every kind of message on the wall to see what sticks,” he said. “There’s not a cookie-cutter Republican ad this year. Whereas the Democratic ads are pretty obvious.”

articles.title: Title IX rollbacks reportedly weaken investigations of discrimination and sexual misconduct
articles.text:
Title IX rollbacks reportedly weaken investigations of discrimination and sexual misconduct – WABE
Title IX rollbacks reportedly weaken investigations of discrimination and sexual misconduct
Closer Look
College Sports
Criminal Justice
Donald Trump
Higher Ed
K-12
Politics
Title IX rollbacks reportedly weaken investigations of discrimination and sexual misconduct
Criminal Justice
Tiffany Griffith
| WABE
October 16th, 2026
Signed into law more than 50 years ago, Title IX provided protections "on the basis of sex" from discrimination and violence "under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance." However, rollbacks under the Trump Administration have reportedly weakened the effectiveness of the law. (Pavel Danilyuk/Element 5 Digital/Pharaoh)
Title IX – it was signed into law by President Richard Nixon more than 50 years ago, but it still has a wide-ranging impact today.
It states: “No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.”
In 2026, Title IX is often at the center of three legal battlegrounds: The responsibility of educational institutions to investigate sexual assault and domestic violence, equality in women’s sports, and the rights of transgender students. But Title IX standards have seen many implementations during the Obama and Biden Administrations, and rollbacks during the Trump Administration.
On today’s special edition of “ Closer Look with Rose Scott,” we examine what these rollbacks have meant for reporting discrimination and sexual violence in schools and sports.
We also spoke with two leaders of an Atlanta-area youth sports nonprofit, as well as a local college student-athlete and youth coach. They discuss mentoring youth to prevent sexual misconduct and the challenges young people face with reporting assault on campus.
GUESTS INCLUDE:
Diana Moskovitz, Investigations Editor for Defector Media
Megan Ballard Mitchell, Title IX Attorney at the Law Offices of M. Ballard Mitchell
C.J. Stewart, co-founder of the Atlanta based L.E.A.D. Center for Youth
Kelli Stewart, CEO of the Atlanta based L.E.A.D. Center for Youth
MacKenna, local college student-athlete and youth coach

articles.title: Hunger strike at Georgia ICE detention center continues
articles.text:
Hunger strike at Georgia ICE detention center continues
Hunger strike at Georgia immigration detention center continues into second week, organizer deported
Immigrants
Immigration Detention
Hunger strike at Georgia immigration detention center continues into second week, organizer deported
Immigration Detention
Emily Wu Pearson
| WABE
October 16th, 2026
The Folkston ICE Processing Center, a private prison operated by The GEO Group, Inc., under contract with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Some detainees here, many of them asylum seekers detained for years at the facility, have been on a hunger strike since Oct. 6. (AP Photo/Mike Stewart)
Immigrants held at the Folkston D. Ray James ICE Processing Facility in Southeast Georgia remain on a hunger strike protesting detention conditions and prolonged detentions.
The strike began on Oct. 6, after 45 men published a letter explaining that many of them are asylum seekers detained for years, some since the Biden administration. They are from countries like Russia, China, Afghanistan, Yemen and Nepal.
They allege insufficient medical care, food that makes people sick and dirty facilities.
GEO Group, the private prison company that runs the facility, deferred questions to Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
ICE said it’s monitoring the situation and will “intervene when it becomes necessary.” A spokesman said 13 people were still on hunger strike. Immigrant rights advocates with the Campaign to Shut Down Folkston ICE Processing Center said many more were involved, with at least 500 people participating at the peak of the protest.
Hunger strike organizer deported
Idris Makhmudov, the author and first signatory of the letter, organized detained immigrants to create a video describing the length of their time and conditions in detention. Advocates said Makhmudov was deported to Russia within the first week of the hunger strike.
“I was studying in university in Russia,” he said during a WABE interview in June. “I was speaking out about the Russian government, Putin’s regime, and of course the war with Ukraine.”
This was in 2023. University students in Russia are not supposed to be drafted, Makhmudov said, but he and other students who were not ethnically Russian were told to join the war effort.
“They just literally threatened me to go to jail,” he said. “They threatened to beat me.”
Makhmudov was detained at the border in 2024 at the appointment he made with Customs and Border Protection to ask for asylum.
“I run from prison to be in prison in another country,” he said.
Makhmudov said his teenage brother, who was detained with him, developed kidney stones and threw up green liquid before he received medical care. He said people in pain were offered ibuprofen as the extent of their medical treatment.
“Everybody, all over the world, we watch American movies, we know all this propaganda about American freedom, justice, law, all these things that never work in Russia,” he said. “We were like, hey, we will come to this country and they will make the right decision. Like they will really look into our case and they will really decide, are we dangerous? Do we need to stay in prison?”
Detained asylum seekers speak out
Asylum-seekers who declare themselves to border agents are often detained.
“It was not unheard of for asylum seekers and especially people who went to a port of entry and asked for asylum at the border to be detained,” said Adriana Heffley, legal director for the Georgia Asylum and Immigration Network. “What we’re seeing right now is more and more immigrants facing years-long detentions.”
Heffley said the Department of Homeland Security can allow asylum seekers who declare themselves at a port of entry to enter the U.S. without being detained and live and work under parole while they wait for their day in immigration court.
Detained in Georgia
ICE detains thousands of immigrants in Georgia, and the numbers are increasing under the second Trump administration. WABE spent time in Stewart County, home to one of the largest immigration detention centers, to better understand what it means for the community — and the people detained there.
That’s what Polina Chertushkina and her husband Andrei Gerdiukov did.
The couple lived in Russia, are Christian, and spoke out against the war in Ukraine. They fled Russia in 2024 and requested asylum at the U.S. border in Texas, received parole, and settled in Brooklyn, New York.
They received work permits, found jobs, paid taxes and went to immigration check-ins while waiting for an asylum hearing set for May 2028.
Earlier this year, Border Patrol stopped the couple while traveling in Florida. They provided all their immigration papers and were detained. Chertushkina was released with an ankle monitor, but Gerdiukov was sent to Alligator Alcatraz and then to Folkston.
He is now part of the hunger strike.
“I love him very much,” she said. “I miss him. When we came to the United States people were welcome, friendly, and they gave us that protection and safety we were seeking.”
Chertushkina said since her husband’s detention, she’s had to sell their car to keep up with the bills. She has seizures, and has asked for Gerdiukov to be transferred closer to New York if he can’t be released on bond.
“When we started hearing about some people who were detained, we were at first thinking they maybe committed a crime or maybe they couldn’t follow their requirements,” she said. “But now I understand that there is no reason for our detention.”
